one_liner: Statically typed embeddable C interpreter; about 4.8x faster than Duktape 1.2.2 on 2015 fib(34), slower than PUC Lua.
what_it_does: Lily is a statically typed scripting language (classes, enums with variants, generics, lambdas, match, coroutines) whose reference implementation is a C11 interpreter shipped as liblily plus a lily executable. Embedding goes through lily.h: fill a lily_config (lily_config_init), create a lily_state with lily_new_state, then lily_load_string / lily_parse_content, and call script functions with lily_call_prepare / lily_call. It is its own language, not a JavaScript or Lua replacement, so swapping it in for Duktape means rewriting scripts and bindings.
how_it_is_fast: The type checker resolves types at parse time, so the emitter writes type-specialised 16-bit register-machine opcodes (o_int_add, o_number_add, o_compare_eq with integer/string/double fast paths) that the VM executes without dynamic type dispatch; integers are unboxed int64 in the register. Calls to a `define` are statically bound (o_call_native) rather than resolved through a global property lookup as Duktape does for fibR. Dispatch is a plain switch loop (no computed goto, no JIT); memory uses refcounting plus a tagged cycle collector for values that can form cycles (gc_start 100, gc_multiplier 4 by default).
when_to_use: You embed a scripting layer in a C or C++ host and want static typing that rejects bad scripts at load time rather than at run time.
You need several independent interpreters in one process (each lily_state is separate; one lily_config can initialise many).
You want a sandbox switch: config.sandbox = 1 loads no predefined modules unless the host opens them, blocks library imports and makes File opens raise RuntimeError.
Integer- and call-heavy script logic where Duktape 1.x-class engines are the alternative; in the 2015 scriptorium fib(34) run Lily took 2.005 s against Duktape's 9.544 s.
You want a small, dependency-free MIT C11 codebase built with CMake that also builds on Windows (MSVC), Linux, BSD, macOS and Haiku.
when_not_to_use: Raw speed is the goal: PUC Lua (1.341 s), LuaJIT (0.111 s with JIT, 0.521 s without), Wren (1.997 s) and AngelScript (2.039 s) were as fast or faster in the same 2015 table, and there is no newer published benchmark for Lily.

You need an existing language and ecosystem (JavaScript, Lua, Python); Lily scripts and libraries are Lily-only and the syntax has changed across releases (2.5 removed `case enum.variant` matching, a breaking change).
Deep recursion: the VM's default call-depth limit is 100 frames (vm->depth_max = 100); scripts must call sys.set_recursion_limit, and lily_config has no field for the host to raise it.
Untrusted scripts that need CPU or memory limits: sandbox mode restricts modules and file access only; no instruction-count or allocation budget hooks are documented in lily.h.
Hash tables exposed to attacker-chosen keys with the default config: the SipHash key defaults to the fixed bytes 1..16, so the host must set config.sipkey itself.

integration.dependencies: none beyond libc (links libdl on Linux and libm off Windows); CMake builds liblily as a shared library by default, static with -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF
integration.min_toolchain: C11 compiler (anonymous unions), CMake 3.10+; the CMake build uses -O2 on GCC/Clang
integration.platforms: Windows (MSVC, MinGW), Linux, *BSD, macOS, Haiku; architecture-neutral C, no JIT
integration.thread_safety: not documented; separate lily_state instances do not share interpreter state, but no locking or thread guarantee is stated

gotchas: Harness flaws behind the number: scriptorium's bench.cc launches the interpreter with system() and sets overhead = 0 (the fib(0) start-up subtraction was never implemented), so start-up and parse time are inside the 2.005 s; the README table keeps each engine's minimum across sessions (Lily 2.31 s in the first logged session, Duktape 9.54 to 14.30 s); the script output is never checked; and its idx::operator< (time, else name) is not a strict weak ordering, so ranks can be misordered even though the times are right.

The baseline was handicapped by its build: Duktape 1.2.2 was compiled from scriptorium's make.bat without DUK_OPT_FASTINT, so all its arithmetic ran in doubles, and fib.js calls a global fibR through a property lookup per call while fib.lly calls a statically bound define.

The measured Lily is a pre-0.15 July 2015 snapshot (old `integer` / `string::format` syntax) linked under the old owner jesserayadkins; the current 2.5 VM is a different code base and has never been benchmarked against Duktape or QuickJS on any page read.

Errors propagate with setjmp/longjmp (lily_jump_setup in lily_vm_execute); C++ foreign functions that hold RAII objects when a Lily exception is raised will skip their destructors. Crash fixes still land in 2026 releases (closure plus high-index global #646, incomplete Hash literal #641).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Lily over AngelScript, Squirrel or mruby (all about 2.0-2.1 s in the same 2015 table, so speed is a wash) when you want a statically typed language with a C11 API, a built-in sandbox flag and an MIT licence; pick Daslang if you want a statically typed embedded language that is measured as fast on current benchmarks, and Lua or Luau if speed and ecosystem matter more than static types.
verified_claims_summary: In r-lyeh's archived scriptorium shootout (July 2015, AMD A10 3.8 GHz, Windows 7 64-bit, VS2015 RC cl /Ox /Oy /MT /DNDEBUG for both), recursive fib(34) as a whole process averaged over 5 launches, best session kept: Lily 2.005 s vs Duktape 1.2.2 9.544 s (about 4.8x, derived from page data) and PUC Lua 1.341 s (Lily about 1.5x slower). The timing includes process start-up and Duktape ran without fastint.
status_note: Actively maintained (quarterly releases, 2.5 on 2026-07-10, last commit 2026-09-22, CI and tracker on GitLab with GitHub as a copy) and MIT with no dependencies, so it is easy to vendor, but its only speed evidence is an eleven-year-old single-kernel run of a pre-1.0 build.
